catalog_quote: Le Kikongo a un accent très prononcé dans les mots et dans la phrase. [...] Règles principales. 1. Dans un même mot, l'accent est généralement sur la syllabe radicale. Ex. Súnda, surpasser; isúndidi, j'ai surpassé; bóka, appeler; bókila, appeler pour; malóngi, doctrine; kúkula, couler. 2. Dans les mots de plus de trois syllabes, il y a un accent secondaire. Ex. Yángalála, se réjouir; bakuntóndelánga, ils l'aiment; búkumúna, détruire; dódokíla, supplier. 3. Dans les mots de deux syllabes, où la première syllabe est un préfixe, l'accent est sur la dernière. Ex. Kitó, cuisse; kikwá, patate; mazú, bruit; mabá, palmiers; kisú, mortier. Mais: Kítu, métamorphose, (de kituka, se changer); lóso, (de lu-oso), riz. 4. Dans les verbes à désinence relative, l'accent se déplace du radical sur l'avant-dernière au prétérit actif et passif. Ex. Bákila, prendre pour; babakídi, ils ont pris pour; bakílu, qui a été pris pour; babóngele, ils ont pris; bambongéle, ils ont pris pour moi, à moi. 5. Les monosyllabes terminant une proposition attirent généralement l'accent sur la syllabe qui précède immédiatement ce monosyllabe.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.translation: Kikongo has a very pronounced accent in words and in the phrase. [...] Main rules. 1. Within a word, the accent is generally on the root syllable. E.g. Súnda 'to surpass'; isúndidi 'I have surpassed'; bóka 'to call'; bókila 'to call for'; malóngi 'doctrine'; kúkula 'to flow'. 2. In words of more than three syllables there is a secondary accent. [...] 3. In words of two syllables where the first syllable is a prefix, the accent is on the last. E.g. Kitó 'thigh'; kikwá 'sweet potato'; mazú 'noise'; mabá 'palm trees'; kisú 'mortar'.
new_statements.citation: Butaye, René (S.J.). 1910. Grammaire congolaise. Roulers: Jules de Meester. Chapitre X 'Accent', pp. 80-81.
new_statements.locator: Chapitre X 'Accent', pp. 80-81 (archive.org scan PDF page 43, two book pages per leaf); printed page numbers verified on the rendered page scan
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again. Opened (archive.org item grammaire-congolayse-butaye, 49 PDF leaves, two printed pages per leaf) and the held page render; re-rendered PDF page 43 at 200 dpi (right-hand page). The page scan shows printed pages "— 80 —" / "— 81 —", heading "CHAPITRE X / ACCENT", opening sentence "Le Kikongo a un accent très prononcé dans les mots et dans la phrase.", then on p. 81 "Règles principales." with rules 1-6 exactly as quoted: "1. Dans un même mot, l'accent est généralement sur la syllabe radicale. Ex. Súnda, surpasser; isúndidi, j'ai surpassé; bóka, appeler; bókila, appeler pour; malóngi, doctrine; kúkula, couler. 2. Dans les mots de plus de trois syllabes, il y a…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Per Butaye 1910 the word accent normally sits on the first syllable of the root (stem-initial), regardless of prefixes; prefix + monosyllabic-stem words are accented on the stem (= final) syllable; the acute marks in the examples are Butaye's. Modern tonological work (Daeleman 1966; Daeleman & Meeussen 1983) analyses the same prominence as high tone, with noun stems bearing H on either the initial or the final stem syllable, which matches Butaye's rules 1 and 3 respectively; the modern sources do not mention stress at all.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Butaye rule 2: 'Dans les mots de plus de trois syllabes, il y a un accent secondaire. Ex. Yángalila, se réjouir; bakuntóndelánga, ils l'aiment; búkumúna, détruire; dódokila, supplier.' (p. 81). Goldsmith 1987 (abstract analysis, p. 98-99) posits secondary accent on the first stem vowel and primary accent on the stem ultima or penult, as a device for tone association.
new_statements.exceptions: Rule 3 counter-examples where a prefix+stem disyllable keeps root accent (Kítu 'metamorphosis' from kítuka; lóso 'rice' from lu-oso); rule 4: verbs with a relative (applicative) suffix shift the accent from the root to the penult in the active and passive preterite (Bákila, babakídi, bakílu, babóngele, bambongéle); p. ~46: in passive preterites 'la pénultième a toujours l'accent tonique'; rule 5: a clause-final monosyllable draws the accent onto the immediately preceding syllable (uenda múna vs. uenda muná nzo; ka bamfutá ko).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('dans un même mot') with an explicit phrase-level rule (5) for clause-final monosyllables; citation forms are verbs in the infinitive and nouns with class prefix. Caveat: 1910 missionary grammar predating any tonal analysis; 'accent' here is perceived prominence and, given the tonological literature (Daeleman & Meeussen 1983: four tonal stem types with H on stem-initial or stem-final syllable), almost certainly denotes the high tone rather than a stress independent of tone. No modern source examined states anything about stress; the most authoritative primary descriptions (Daeleman 1966; Daeleman & Meeussen 1983) treat Ntandu as a tone language and are silent on stress.
new_statements.identity_note: All usable sources describe Kintandu (Ntandu), the Kisantu-region dialect (Guthrie H16g), which Glottolog 5.1 lists as one of five varieties of Eastern Kikongo [east2782] alongside Kimbata, Kimbeko, Kimpangu and Kinkanu (no separate glottocodes; the Glottolog bibliography codes these works as 'Eastern Kikongo [NOCODE_Eastern-Kikongo]', which is why our source list showed 0 refs). Butaye 1910 calls the variety 'haut-kikongo' (right bank of the Inkisi, bounded by Stanley Pool and the Nsele), i.e. the Kisantu Jesuit-mission dialect; the archive.org item and Glottolog both identify it as Kintandu/Ntandu. No phonological description of Kimpangu, Kimbata, Kimbeko or Kinkanu was found.

tone_statements.citation: Donnelly, Kevin Gerard. 1982. A comparative study of tone and intonation in seven Kongo dialects. PhD thesis, School of Oriental and African Studies, University of London. 522 pp. DOI 10.25501/SOAS.00028544.
tone_statements.quote: (b) to demonstrate that in certain cases the pitch features of kiKongo are difficult to analyse in terms of tone, and may therefore warrant a pitch-accent description; [...] There is usually (but not always) only one high pitch per word (15.7). 64% (on average) of all high pitches occurred on the 'root-syllable*, the first syllable of the root or stem, while 72% (on average) of all words had high pitch on the root-syllable (see Appendix 7/3 and 15.7). Pitchmeter tracings, apart from validating the pitch-marking used, showed that in 84% of all words in a sample passage highest intensity occurred on the root-syllable. [...] These facts suggest that we can postulate a simple, yet comprehensive, rule for high pitch occurrence, namely, ‘high pitch usually occurs on the root-syllable'. This is taken as the basic pattern.

sources.note: Chapitre X 'Accent', pp. 80-81: Kikongo has a very pronounced accent in words and phrases; in a word the accent is generally on the root syllable (Súnda, isúndidi, bóka, bókila, malóngi, kúkula); words of more than three syllables have a secondary accent; disyllables of prefix + monosyllabic stem accent the final syllable (Kitó, kikwá, mazú); relative-suffix verbs shift accent to the penult in the preterite; clause-final monosyllables attract the accent to the preceding syllable. Elsewhere (p. ~46): 'Dans ces prétérits passifs, la pénultième a toujours l'accent tonique.' No mention of tone as…

sources.citation: Goldsmith, John. 1987. Tone and accent, and getting the two together. Proceedings of the Thirteenth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society: 88-104.
sources.tag: read: notes on stress
sources.note: Theoretical re-analysis of Kintandu noun tone (data from Daeleman 1983 ITL) as tone-to-accent association: 'there are two levels of accent, primary and secondary. The first vowel of the stem always receives secondary accent, while the primary accent falls either on the ultimate or penultimate syllable of the stem' (pp. 98-99); frames the question 'What is it that makes us think that Kintandu is not just a stress system?'. Abstract, tone-attracting accent, not a phonetic stress claim.
sources.venue: Proceedings of the Thirteenth Annual Meeting of the Berkeley Linguistics Society: 88-104

sources.quote: (b) to demonstrate that in certain cases the pitch features of kiKongo are difficult to analyse in terms of tone, and may therefore warrant a pitch-accent description; [...] There is usually (but not always) only one high pitch per word (15.7). 64% (on average) of all high pitches occurred on the 'root-syllable*, the first syllable of the root or stem, while 72% (on average) of all words had high pitch on the root-syllable (see Appendix 7/3 and 15.7). sources.note: Argues that kiKongo pitch features, hitherto analysed as lexical tone, are better described as a pitch accent system with an intonational overlay: usually one high pitch per word, basically on the root-initial syllable (64% of high pitches, 72% of words), with 'anomalous' variants (leftward shift before locative/genitive/connective elements, high on the final syllable, or no high pitch) and 'bridging' (L assimilating to surrounding Hs) tied to focus/emphasis; comparison of Laman's, Carter's and Daeleman's tone-classes reduces them to two main accentual classes, rising (low-initial) vs falling…
